extracted.intended_audience: environmental lawyers, policy advocates, and EPA rulemaking staff participating in notice-and-comment on EPA greenhouse gas rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A formal legal/commentary submission opposing EPA's proposed rescission of its 2009 greenhouse gas Endangerment Finding under CAA §202(a)(1), assessing statutory interpretation, scientific evidence, and administrative-law requirements. Targets EPA rulemaking record and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis contribution of vehicle water vapor emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehicle and human-activity water vapor emissions do not meaningfully increase atmospheric water vapor because water vapor has a very short atmospheric lifetime (days) and anthropogenic inputs are many orders of magnitude smaller than natural evaporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hydrologic-cycle science (evaporation, precipitation, Clausius–Clapeyron relation) and quantitative comparisons (e.g., estimated vehicle water vapor production ≈ 6.5x10^11 kg/year; percent of atmospheric water at a moment; percent of annual atmospheric cycling; percent of hydrologic system stock) to show such emissions are truly de minimis and therefore cannot satisfy the statutory 'contribute' element for regulation of water vapor. Cite peer-reviewed literature and authoritative sources (NASA, USGS, EIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of separating contribution and endangerment findings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is lawful and reasonable for EPA to evaluate Section 202(a)(1)’s contribution and endangerment prongs separately—i.e., determine whether emissions from new motor vehicles 'contribute' to dangerous air pollution distinct from whether the pollution 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger' health or welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory text supports separate inquiries; administrative practice and logic allow contribution analysis to consider larger aggregates and not be forced into a single combined test. EPA must defend its analytic choices but may separate the prongs without collapsing them into a single metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual interpretation of 'contribute' requires considering all sources and not limiting to mobile sources alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress used the term 'contribute' and separately referenced 'air pollution' and 'air pollutant,' EPA should consider all sources of the pollution (domestic and international; new and existing) when assessing whether new motor vehicles 'contribute' to the relevant pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on plain-text statutory reading: absence of further qualification around 'contribute' indicates Congress intended a broad consideration. Do not restrict endangerment to only sources regulated under Section 202(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective grouping of well-mixed greenhouse gases is lawful
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA properly evaluated the six well-mixed greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6) collectively as the subject 'air pollutant' because they share characteristics (multi-year/century atmospheric lifetimes; become well-mixed; absorb outgoing infrared radiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating substances as a single pollutant is authorized by the Clean Air Act definition of 'air pollutant' as 'any air pollution agent or combination of such agents.' Use agency precedent where EPA regulates groups (hydrocarbons, VOCs, particulate matter) to justify grouping when common characteristics and common contribution to harm exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: No specific numerical bright line required for 'contribution' determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Contribution determinations under Section 202(a) do not require a particular numerical threshold or precise percentage to be reached; numerical percentages are not treated as precise bright lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency may rely on qualitative and quantitative evidence and reasonable proxies; it should explain its reasoning but need not produce a single magic number to show 'contribute.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing fleet emissions are a reasonable surrogate for new vehicle emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Using emissions data from the existing U.S. vehicle fleet is a reasonable proxy for emissions from new vehicles because fleet turnover occurs on a time frame short compared to the time period relevant to endangerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support surrogate choice with turnover/lifespan data and historical emissions trends; show that the existing fleet closely approximates emissions of new vehicles due to production and turnover dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency may rely on aggregate or nationwide emissions when evaluating contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Contribution can be assessed by reference to total greenhouse gas emissions from all relevant sources (domestic and international) rather than only those emissions that will be directly regulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why aggregate measures capture the pollution problem Congress intended EPA to address; show mathematical/logical consistency (e.g., subset contribution to an aggregate is contribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative-law requirement to consider and explain departures from prior determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: If EPA intends to depart from prior findings (like the 2009 Endangerment Finding), it must acknowledge prior conclusions, explain why it is changing course in light of the record, and provide reasoned analysis; failure to do so is arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite precedent and demonstrate that the agency neglected to address substantial prior evidence and determinations reaffirming endangerment (2009–2024). Provide specific examples of ignored findings to show inadequacy of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment finding must be grounded in current, peer-reviewed scientific evidence and authoritative assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: An affirmative endangerment finding must be supported by the body of scientific evidence—including peer-reviewed literature and assessments such as IPCC reports, the U.S. National Climate Assessment, and National Academies reports—that documents GHGs' harms to climate, health, and welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the latest consensus assessments and peer-reviewed literature to show causal links between anthropogenic GHGs and impacts (temperature rise, sea level, extreme events, ecosystem harms). Reference recent NASEM conclusions that strengthen the 2009 Finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must not rely on flawed or procedurally illegitimate reports without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency cannot permissibly base action on an 'illegally conducted and substantively flawed' draft report (e.g., the Draft CWG Report) without critically evaluating its methodology and responding to its flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify substantive and procedural defects in such reports; explain why reliance would be arbitrary; use both methodological critique and record-based rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative magnitude and atmospheric lifetime are key for contribution analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a source 'contributes' depends on both the quantity of emissions relative to natural/background stocks/fluxes and the atmospheric lifetime of the pollutant (short-lived vs long-lived).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lifetime data (days vs years to centuries) and comparative magnitude calculations (percent of atmospheric burden, percent of annual cycling) to assess whether a particular anthropogenic emission stream meaningfully alters concentrations and thus contributes to endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for indirect/feedback effects (GHG-induced increases in atmospheric water vapor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses must distinguish between direct emissions (vehicle water vapor) and indirect consequences of other GHGs (CO2-driven warming increasing atmospheric water vapor via Clausius–Clapeyron), recognizing that water vapor increase is largely a feedback rather than a primary driver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute responsibility correctly: show that long-lived GHG emissions increase atmospheric capacity for water vapor and that vehicle water vapor itself is not the driver. Cite IPCC/NASA explanations of feedback amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical/mathematical consistency in contribution arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and scientific reasoning about contribution must be logically coherent—e.g., four elements that are part of a larger six-element set can plausibly 'contribute' to the larger set; excluding members of the set does not negate contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple analogies and mathematical logic to rebut claims that aggregating pollutants is impermissible or 'apples and oranges.' Demonstrate set/subset reasoning and percent-accounting where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory purpose and legislative history support incremental regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory purpose (protecting and enhancing national air quality) and decisions like Massachusetts support the proposition that incremental domestic emission reductions are meaningful and lawful even if global problems persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite legislative purpose provisions (42 U.S.C. §§ 7401(a)(2), (b)(1)) and Massachusetts precedent to rebut futility arguments; emphasize that regulation of one domestic source can slow global increases and spur broader international action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebutting 'futility' requires empirical and legal evidence, not mere assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that regulating a sector would be 'futile' must be supported by legal authority and empirical evidence; absent such support, futility is not a valid basis to rescind a finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide data showing sectoral significance (e.g., transportation ~28–29% of U.S. GHGs; motor vehicles as lion's share) and international examples of regulation to show meaningfulness of U.S. action. Show lack of caselaw or statutory basis for 'futility' defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbon leakage is not relevant to the statutory questions in Section 202(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about carbon leakage (production shifting abroad) fall outside the narrow statutory questions of whether air pollution may reasonably be anticipated to endanger health/welfare and whether new vehicles emit pollutants that contribute to that pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that vehicle standards regulate emissions from vehicles driven in the U.S.; supply evidence (e.g., EU carbon-leakage lists excluding motor vehicles) and reasoning that leakage does not negate domestic contribution or endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency should use up-to-date and transparent empirical data to support or rebut claims
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA and commenters should rely on recent, publicly available emissions and fleet data (e.g., EIA, FHWA) and clearly state assumptions when making aggregate calculations (e.g., gallons consumed, kg water per gallon, vehicle counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide citations and arithmetic demonstrating trends (e.g., CO2 emissions 2010 vs 2024; registered vehicle counts; vehicle lifespans) and explain why those data undercut claims that earlier proxies were unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedential administrative practice of regulating diverse chemical groups supports treating GHGs collectively
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has long regulated diverse chemical groups (hydrocarbons, VOCs, PM) as single pollutants when they share properties relevant to the pollutant's impacts; the same practice supports treating well-mixed GHGs together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite historical Federal Register actions and relevant CAA provisions showing examples and legal authority for grouped regulation; emphasize common property (formation of ozone, small particle size, well-mixed radiative forcing) as justificatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must respond to record evidence reaffirming past findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When the record contains multiple subsequent EPA findings and external authoritative reports that reaffirm the 2009 finding, an agency proposing rescission must meaningfully engage with and respond to that body of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific post-2009 EPA findings and authoritative reports (NASEM 2025, NCA, IPCC assessments) and explain how the agency's proposal fails to address or distinguish those materials; show that unexplained omission renders action arbitrary.
